leads.text: jose/jwe.py:_decrypt_and_auth verifies the JWE Authenticated-Encryption (CBC+HMAC) auth tag with a plain Python `!=` comparison instead of a constant-time comparison, unlike the equivalent HMAC-signature check elsewhere in the same codebase (jose/backends/native.py uses hmac.compare_digest). This is a missing timing-safe-comparison control on a security-critical MAC verification.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (m:CpgMethod{scan_id:$scan_id})-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall{scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE m.full_name='jose/jwe.py:<module>._decrypt_and_auth' RETURN c.name,c.code,c.line ORDER BY c.line → result includes {c.name:'<operator>.notEquals', c.code:'auth_tag != auth_tag_check', c.line:247} inside `_decrypt_and_auth` (defined jose/jwe.py line 215). For comparison, the sibling HMAC-verify path DOES use a constant-time check: query on CpgCall name='compare_digest' returned exactly one row: {file_path:'jose/backends/native.py', code:'hmac.compare_digest(sig, self.sign(msg))', line:69} — showing the safe pattern exists in this codebase but is absent from the JWE auth-tag check.

leads.text: JWS signature verification does not bind the declared `alg` header (fully attacker-controlled, taken from the untrusted token) to the actual type/intent of the key material supplied by the caller. jws.py:_sig_matches_keys calls jwk.construct(key, alg) for any `key` that is not already a jose Key instance, and jwk.construct (jose/jwk.py lines 63-79) picks the Key class purely from the `alg` string via get_key(), with no check that raw key bytes/PEM/dict actually correspond to that algorithm family. Combined with _verify_signature only enforcing an algorithm whitelist when the caller explicitly supplies `algorithms` (`algorithms is not None and alg not in algorithms` at line 258 — skipped entirely when algorithms is None/omitted), this is the classic JWT 'algorithm confusion' gap: a caller who stores an RSA/EC public key as raw PEM/dict and does not pass a restrictive `algorithms` allow-list can have an attacker-forged HS256 token (using the public PEM bytes as the HMAC secret) accepted as valid.
leads.evidence: Query on jose/jws.py:<module>._verify_signature CONTAINS_CALL calls returned: {code:'alg = header.get("alg")', line:254}; {code:'algorithms is not None and alg not in algorithms', line:258}; {code:'raise JWSError("The specified alg value is not allowed")', line:259}; {code:'_sig_matches_keys(keys, signing_input, signature, alg)', line:263}. Query on jose/jws.py:<module>._sig_matches_keys returned: {code:'not isinstance(key, Key)', line:211}; {code:'jwk.construct(key, alg)', line:212}; {code:'key.verify(signing_input, signature)', line:214} — key type is only checked for being a pre-built Key object, never checked against `alg`. Query on jose/jwk.py:<module>.construct returned {code:'key_class = get_key(algorithm)', line:76}; {code:'key_class(key_data, algorithm)', line:79} — construct() instantiates whatever class `get_key(alg)` maps to, with no validation that key_data matches that key family.

leads.text: The same missing algorithm/key-type binding exists on the JWE decryption path: jose/jwe.py decrypt() builds the content-encryption/key-wrap key via `jwk.construct(key, alg)` at line 108 using the attacker-controlled `alg` header value from the untrusted JWE token, with no check that the caller-supplied `key` object was intended for that algorithm (e.g. an attacker could flip the header's alg from an asymmetric key-wrap algorithm to 'dir' to force the server's key bytes to be reinterpreted directly as the content-encryption key).
leads.evidence: Query on jose/jwe.py:<module>.decrypt CONTAINS_CALL calls returned: {code:'alg = header["alg"]', line:97}; {code:'alg not in ALGORITHMS.SUPPORTED', line:99} (whitelist checked only against the global list of all supported algs, not against what the key was issued for); {code:'key = jwk.construct(key, alg)', line:108}; {code:'alg == ALGORITHMS.DIR', line:127}.

leads.text: jose/jwt.py:_validate_at_hash compares the token's `at_hash` claim against the locally computed expected hash with a plain `!=` rather than a constant-time comparison, a smaller-scale instance of the same missing-timing-safe-comparison pattern found in the JWE auth-tag check.
leads.evidence: Query on jose/jwt.py:<module>._validate_at_hash CONTAINS_CALL calls returned: {code:'expected_hash = calculate_at_hash(access_token, ALGORITHMS.HASHES[algorithm])', line:452}; {code:'claims["at_hash"] != expected_hash', line:457}; {code:'raise JWTClaimsError("at_hash claim does not match access_token.")', line:458}.

leads.text: No code anywhere in the codebase implements the JWS/JWE 'crit' (critical header parameter) extension check required by RFC 7515 §4.1.11 / RFC 7516 — an implementation MUST reject a JOSE object that declares a 'crit' header naming an extension it does not understand. This control is entirely absent, so jws.py/jwe.py will silently process tokens carrying unrecognized critical header extensions instead of rejecting them.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall{scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'crit' RETURN c.file_path,c.code,c.line → row_count 0 (no match) across the whole scan.

leads.text: jose/jwt.py decode() builds a 'defaults' options dict with verify_signature/verify_exp/verify_aud/verify_iss/etc all True, then does defaults.update(options) with the caller-supplied options and passes verify_signature straight into jws.verify(token, key, algorithms, verify=verify_signature) -- so any caller can flip verify_signature/verify_exp/verify_aud to False and fully disable JWT signature/claim verification for that call. This is exercised directly in tests/test_firebase.py, which calls jwt.decode(firebase_token, cert, algorithms='RS256', options={'verify_exp': False, 'verify_aud': False}) against a real captured production-style Firebase token, demonstrating the disable-knob is live and reachable from entry rather than dead code.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.file_path='jose/jwt.py' AND c.line >= 100 AND c.line <= 150 -> rows show defaults dict literal with tmp0["verify_signature"]=True etc (uid 0bfc00f814a7ecba0470dd981d198f5a6c4a52a6), then 'defaults.update(options)' (line 140), 'verify_signature = defaults.get("verify_signature", True)' (line 142), and 'jws.verify(token, key, algorithms, verify = verify_signature)' (line 145), all reachable_from_entry=true. Query on tests/test_firebase.py -> uid 40aa705fb7a6af46bc6d1458adcfad786ff984b0 c.code="jwt.decode(firebase_token, firebase_certs[...], algorithms = \"RS256\", options = {\"verify_exp\":False, \"verify_aud\":False})" at line 27.

leads.text: Declared dependency ecdsa with version constraint "!= 0.15" (i.e. any other version is accepted) is the python-ecdsa package, which upstream has acknowledged is NOT resistant to the Minerva timing side-channel attack against ECDSA signing/verification (CVE-2024-23342). The version spec only excludes 0.15 and does not pin to a patched/mitigated release, so a vulnerable version can be installed. This is a components-with-known-vulnerabilities issue (CWE-937/CWE-208) independent of any request flow, consistent with jose/backends/ecdsa_backend.py using this library for signature operations.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name, d.version -> row {"name":"ecdsa","version":"!= 0.15"}. Also confirmed jose/backends/ecdsa_backend.py exists among production files (MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.file_path STARTS WITH 'jose/' ... -> includes jose/backends/ecdsa_backend.py).

leads.text: Declared dependency cryptography is pinned to ==42.0.4, a release from February 2024. As of the scan date (Oct 2026) this pin is roughly two and a half years stale, predating multiple subsequent `cryptography` security releases; the project should be upgraded and re-audited for CVEs fixed after 42.0.4.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name, d.version -> row {"name":"cryptography","version":"==42.0.4"}.

leads.text: Declared dependencies rsa, pyasn1, and pycryptodome all have an empty version string in the manifest -- i.e. no version constraint at all. This allows dependency resolution to silently pick very old releases, including versions of `rsa` affected by CVE-2020-13757 (PKCS#1 v1.5 ciphertext integer-overflow leading to incorrect encryption/decryption). Unpinned crypto-library dependencies are a components-with-known-vulnerabilities / supply-chain risk regardless of request flow.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name, d.version -> rows {"name":"rsa","version":""}, {"name":"pyasn1","version":""}, {"name":"pycryptodome","version":""}.

leads.text: Declared dependency docopt is pinned to ==0.6.2, the last release of a project that has been unmaintained since 2014. It is an end-of-life component with no security support; any future vulnerability in it will never be patched upstream.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name, d.version -> row {"name":"docopt","version":"==0.6.2"}.

leads.text: Declared dependency PyYAML is pinned to ==5.4.1 (released 2021), an outdated version relative to current releases. No call to yaml.load/yaml.safe_load was found anywhere in the scanned source, so this appears to be a transitive/dev-only dependency rather than something exercised by application code -- flagged for completeness as an outdated declared component, not as an active code-execution sink.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name, d.version -> row {"name":"PyYAML","version":"==5.4.1"}. Follow-up: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'yaml.load' OR c.code CONTAINS 'yaml.safe_load' ... -> 0 rows.
